newsitem.title: FRANCE: France asks EU on 3.9 bln CL emergency aid.
newsitem.headline: France asks EU on 3.9 bln CL emergency aid.

text.p: The French government hopes to get the green light from the European Commission later on Wednesday for an emergency state aid of 3.9 billion francs ($765.5 million) for state bank Credit Lyonnais, business daily La Tribune said.
The newspaper said the 3.9 billion francs for which Paris was seeking clearance was emergency aid only and could be followed up by a new rescue package.

Sources close to the talks had raised the possibility of a new rescue plan involving a 10-billion-franc recapitalisation, the paper said, adding that Lyonnais chairman Jean Peyrelevade met EU Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert on Tuesday. ($ = 5.094 French Francs)
Van Miert is scheduled to hold a news conference on Credit Lyonnais later on Wednesday, which is the day he and the other members of the Commission hold their weekly meeting.

French newspapers including La Tribune said Van Miert was expected to ask his colleagues to decide swiftly in favour of the emergency aid but also to open an inquiry under European Union state aid rules into the wider rescue plan in the pipeline.

Les Echos newspaper said 2.9 billion of the 3.9 billion francs in emergency aid would go direct to the bank and the rest to the EPFR state holding company involved in selling Credit Lyonnais assets under a rescue package that got EU approval in July 1995.
The bank has postponed a board meeting where its first-half results were due to be approved to October 3 from September 26.

The bank ran into trouble after a runaway expansion in the late 1980s and early 1990s which gave it a fleeting moment of glory as Europe's largest bank but ran up losses of more than 20 billion francs between 1992 and 1994.

One rescue package was drawn up in 1994 and another followed in 1995, getting EU approval in return for a pledge to sell off many of the bank's assets, notably outside France, and to gear the bank up for privatisation after the year 2000.
